resources.string: MAP vs. barometric difference (plus ±%1$s from the source)
the pressure estimated from GPS altitude
MAP at %1$s, no barometric pressure to compare
MAP close to barometric pressure, inconclusive
No MAP readings (PID 0B) arrived with the ignition on, so there is nothing to compare.
With the engine off, MAP read %1$s (%2$s).
No reference barometric pressure: the ECU did not report PID 33, the phone has no barometer and there was no GPS altitude.
The reference was %1$s: %2$s. The difference is %3$s; with no vacuum, %4$s is expected, plus ±%5$s from the source.
%1$s equals atmospheric pressure at an altitude of about %2$s.
Reads low: consistent with a miscalibrated MAP sensor (P0106) or a low 5 V reference. The MAP shares that reference with the TPS: if the TPS also reads low, check the shared reference.
Reads high: consistent with a miscalibrated MAP sensor (P0106), a high signal (P0108) or an open sensor ground.
Matches within the band: the MAP reads pressure correctly with the engine off.
Many ECUs compute barometric pressure from the MAP sensor itself when the ignition is turned on: a match does not rule out a miscalibrated MAP.
Matches %1$s but not %2$s: with references that disagree, no conclusion is possible.
The difference exceeds the typical band but fits within the source uncertainty: this reference cannot settle it.
MAP varied by %1$s with the engine off: unstable signal, consistent with a loose connection
Check that the adapter is still connected and that the ECU reports MAP (PID 0B)
Turn on phone location (for GPS altitude) or use a phone with a barometer, then repeat the test
Measure the MAP 5 V reference, ground and signal with the multimeter (MAP template)
Repeat with the phone barometer or the ECU barometric pressure (PID 33): both are more accurate references than altitude
To rule out a miscalibrated MAP, repeat the test with a phone that has a barometer
MAP equals an altitude of about %1$s
